input: In this example we consider a single-stage compressor that raises natural gas from 1 bar to 4 bar, a duty that is representative of a wide range of gas-handling applications. The inlet temperature of the gas is 293 K. If the compression is imagined to take place isentropically, with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, the discharge temperature that emerges from the calculation is 435 K. It is, however, essential to appreciate what this figure does and does not represent. The isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses, which means that it paints a somewhat idealised picture of the machine, and the installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher than the calculated value. In other words, the number that comes out of the isentropic calculation should be read as a benchmark arrived at under deliberately simplified assumptions, rather than as a faithful prediction of what a thermometer at the discharge of the real machine would actually register. The gap between the two temperatures is where all of the real-world imperfections of the machine reside, even though the calculation itself does not attempt to itemise them or to assign a share of the difference to any particular source of loss. There is also a broader methodological point worth making here, namely that idealised calculations of this type are valuable precisely because they strip away the complications of the real machine and expose the part of the behaviour that depends only on the stated pressures, the inlet temperature, and the properties of the gas, leaving everything else to be accounted for by measurement.
target: A single-stage compressor raises natural gas from 1 bar to 4 bar. A single stage takes the whole pressure rise in one machine, with no intercooling between stages. From an inlet temperature of 293 K, isentropic compression with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4 gives a discharge temperature of 435 K. The heat-capacity ratio is the ratio of the specific heat at constant pressure to the specific heat at constant volume, and it fixes how strongly the temperature responds to the pressure change in the isentropic relation. The isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses. Isentropic compression is compression without heat transfer and without irreversibility, so no allowance stands in the estimate for friction in the bearings, leakage past the seals, or irreversibility in the gas path. Each of those effects, where it acts, converts work into internal energy of the gas and raises the discharge temperature above the isentropic value. The installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher, and the isentropic value is therefore a reference calculated for an idealised machine rather than a prediction of the installed discharge temperature. The brief quantifies none of the loss effects, and the difference between the calculated and measured temperatures cannot be divided among them from the stated data. The discharge temperature is the quantity that downstream cooling and the machine's own materials limits are set against, so the distinction between the calculated reference and the measured value is the operative point of the example. At the stated scope, the result is an isentropic discharge temperature for the specified pressure rise, with the installed machine running hotter for reasons the estimate does not attempt to cost.
